newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-RBA takes market by surprise again with cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-RBA takes market by surprise again with cut.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) took financial markets by surprise again on Wednesday, cutting official interest rates for the fifth time in a year.
The cut itself, which reduced the bank's official cash rate by 50 basis points to 5.0 percent, was widely expected following the release of inflation and wages data last week.
But the bank had generally been expected to wait until after its next board meeting on August 5 before making its move.

"This change, like the four previous reductions in interest rates over the past year, is based on the improving picture for Australia's medium-term inflation performance, which opens up scope for faster growth and employment," the central bank said.
Economists welcomed the rate cut but said that the timing of the cut caught the market off guard.
"The only oddity in the whole thing was the timing," said Michael Blythe, senior economist with the Commonwealth Bank.

"Just about everbody has been expecting a rate cut in the very short term and the RBA has come through. Certainly with inflation dead in the water and unemployment still high there seems to be no reason not to cut rates," Blythe said.
Some economists said the bank's bullish reasoning for its fifth rate cut may even suggest the bank believed there was room for a further reduction in interest rates.
"There might be some attempt to price in another rate cut," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust.
Tony Meer, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenefll, said the bank's comment that the economy had room to grow in the next two to three years without threatening inflation was significant.
"It suggests the bank sees enough room for yet another easing, if not two," Meer said.
The RBA noted that underlying inflation in the year to June was 1.7 percent and that it expected underlying inflation inflation to stay below two percent into 1998.
Underlying inflation strips out volatile elements of the consumer price index, such as mortgage rates.
The bank also said economic growth in 1997 had been picking up, but that it remained moderate. GDP grew at an annual rate of 2.4 percent in the March quarter.
"The crucial test for monetary policy is to have the setting that will best contribute to low inflation and economic growth in the long run," the RBA said.
"...Monetary policy should not stand in the way of a period of stronger growth that can be accommodated without breaching the inflation objective," the bank said.

The bank said that although earlier rate cuts were still working their way through the economy, it believed the latest cut would not fuel inflation. "The balance of risks at this time is such as to favour this further easing of monetary policy."
The markets had already priced in a half point cut in rates.

The Australian dollar initially dropped on the news but by mid-morning had bounced back to US$0.7450, almost where it was before the cut was announced at 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT). It hit a low of $0.7395. Bonds rallied on the news but gains were quickly pared back and the 10-year government bond was quoted at 6.47 percent mid-morning, having briefly dipped below 6.40 percent.
The All Ordinaries share index was up 4.1 points at 2736 at mid-morning, well off its high of 2747.6, led by interest rate sensitive banks. The cut was announced before the market opened.

Treasurer Peter Costello said Australia was in a strong position after the rate cut, which he said reflected the government's policy of keeping interest rates low. He also said the cut posed no threat to the Australian dollar.
"Having got interest rates down, I can assure you it is very much part of our policy to keep them there," he told reporters.
He said rate cuts announced in late 1996 were still working their way through the economy and that the benefits of the remaining two rate cuts were yet to materialise.

He said Australia now had a very good outlook for the coming year. "This is a conjunction of very significant economic news which sets Australia up for a very good outlook over the forthcoming year," Costello said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
